The DQN Workshop

A Deep Q-Network learns by grading its own guesses. After every move it asks one question: how far off was my guess, compared with what actually happened plus my guess about what happens next? Then it nudges its weights to shrink that gap. The three stations below let you poke at that loop until it clicks.

The Bench

Set up one moment of the game, pick a move, and watch a single update happen with real numbers from a real network. Change anything (the board, the move, a knob) and the whole worked solution recomputes.

  3. The target

    What q should have been, in hindsight: the reward you actually got, plus the discounted value of where you ended up.

  4. The gap

    Guess against target. This single number is what the whole network gets adjusted to shrink.

  5. Nudge the weights

    Backpropagation works out, for every one of the network’s weights, which direction would move q toward the target. Each nudge moves every weight a tiny step that way.

    Press a nudge button to watch the guess move toward the target.

Ripple Tank

A simpler world: one cherry worth +10, one ghost worth −10. At the start no square knows anything, so the map is blank. The only true information enters where rewards happen, then leaks backward into the guesses, one step at a time.

−100+10
Tapping a square will place
Brain

Things to try

  • Press Sweep a few times. Each sweep grades every square once, against a frozen snapshot of the previous sweep, and the color spreads exactly one square further from the cherry. That is the reward leaking backward.
  • Slide future discount down to 0.5. Far squares barely care about the cherry anymore: the glow fades fast with distance.
  • Switch to Network and press One step. A single update tints many squares at once, because they share weights. That sharing is why DQN uses a network: it can guess about squares it has never visited.
  • After it has learned, move the cherry. Watch the old knowledge get overwritten.

Arcade

Now the whole machine: a brand-new network plays this maze, stores every moment in a replay memory, and learns from random handfuls of it using exactly the update from the Bench. It starts out walking into walls and ghosts. Keep an eye on the exam line under the stats: expect it to start climbing after roughly 20,000 steps, a few minutes on Turbo. Or load the trained brain to skip ahead.

The line is the exam: every 2,500 steps the agent plays the same 10 games with no random moves and no learning, which shows what it has really learned. Dots are practice games, which include random moves. Dashed line: random play.

Experiments

Each one changes a knob and marks the moment on the chart so you can see the effect. Run them on a brain that is already learning (or load the trained one) and give each a minute on Turbo.

Built from scratch for this page: an 11,908-weight network with hand-written backpropagation, Adam, replay memory, a frozen target copy and Double DQN, all running in your browser. Same algorithm as the pacdqn project, smaller maze.
